# **Precious metal report** _Gold, silver, platinum and palladium September 2011_ **David Jollie david.jollie@mitprecious.com Tel: +44 20 7489 6767** **24 October 2011** #### **New York:** - September was a negative month for precious metals prices with all four of the main metals (and rhodium and ruthenium) losing significant ground. In fact the only precious metal which appreciated in price during the month was the generallyoverlooked iridium. The main news stories concerned two factors: worries over a slowing global economy and the possibility that the major developed economies might tip into recession in the coming months; and outright fear that the European debt crisis might drive a sovereign default or a fullyfledged banking crisis. • The annual LBMA conference was held (jointly with the LPPM) in Montreal from the 18th to the 20th of September. Few new opinions or facts were revealed relating to the gold market which was held with gold trading close to $1,800 per ounce. At the start of the conference, attendees forecast a gold price of $2,075 at the time of the next conference (November 2012). By the end of the conference, this forecast had fallen to a still bullish $2,019. However, although the mood was positive, when compared to a year earlier, the conference attendees were rather less universally bullish on this occasion. • Gold has established a significant price premium to platinum. We prefer to look at the spread between these materials in preference to the ratio as it contains more useful information. Specifically, the spread is currently acting as a fear gauge, showing market stress. Although the gold price fell heavily in September, the spread over the platinum price widened as investors became more risk averse, with gold’s safe haven characteristics insulating it from some of the frenzied selling. For platinum to reestablish parity with gold seems to require reversion to a focus on platinum’s fundamentals or at least a belief that the world economy could start to grow at a reasonable pace once again. 200 Park Avenue, New York, NY 10166 0130 Tel: +1 212 878 4122 #### **London:** 4th Floor, St Martins Court, 10 Paternoster Row, London EC4M 7BB Tel: +44 20 7489 6767 #### **Hong Kong:** Suite 1306, Two Exchange Square, 8 Connaught Place, Central, Hong Kong Tel: +852 2899 2026 #### **Tokyo:** 2-1 Ohtemachi 1-Chome, Chiyoda-Ku, Tokyo 100 Tel: +81 33 285 3407 #### **Singapore:** 80 Robinson Road, #15-02, Singapore, 068898 Tel: +65 6372 8050 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **24 October 2011** ## **Contents** |**Overview**|**4**| |---|---| |**Gold**

3 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **24 October 2011** ## **Overview** September was a very poor month for precious metals prices with all four of the main metals (and rhodium and ruthenium) losing significant ground. In fact the only precious metal which appreciated in price during the month was the generally-overlooked iridium. The main news stories concerned two factors: worries over a slowing global economy and the possibility that the major developed economies at least might tip into recession in the coming months; and outright fear that the European debt crisis might drive a sovereign default or a fully-fledged banking crisis. In this increasingly risk-averse environment, a wide range of assets were sold, driving prices lower. Almost as importantly, the Dollar strengthened against most currencies, reflecting its real safe haven status as a destination for scared investors. This created a headwind for all commodity prices and generated much of the initial price weakness. The decision to link the Swiss Franc to the Euro (which was taken on the 6th of September) reinforced the US Dollar’s short-term allure, and, although we see this decision as positive for gold prices eventually, prices of all of the precious metals sagged further. **_Figure 2_** _: Although a firmer US Dollar was not the only cause of lower metals prices in September, a “flight to quality” and away from the Euro did have a significant negative impact on prices._ In our August monthly report, we commented on the growing likelihood of further quantitative easing taking place in the USA. On the 21st of September, the US Federal Reserve duly announced the debut of “Operation Twist”. This attempts to lower longer term interest rates by extending the time profile of treasuries owned by the Reserve over the next nine months. When combined with the avowed intention of maintaining interest rates at very low levels, th

is should make borrowing cheaper and could therefore support the housing market and the rest of the US economy. However, following this announcement, many asset markets plunged in value. In part this may have been due to the realisation that QE3 might not now happen for quite some time. However, the more important reason seems to have been the tacit acknowledgement by the Federal Reserve of the unhealthy state of the US economy. With concerns growing over European sovereign debt and the health of an increasing number of European banks, the Dollar strengthened nonetheless and commodity prices fell further. Even gold suffered from margin-driven selling. The prospects of QE3 do not, though, seem to have disappeared entirely. The UK has decided to start a new round of quantitative easing itself to address the weakness in its economy. The European Central Bank may yet have to reduce interest rates and start some quantitative easing in order to support the wider European economy. And, although, the political environment may make it unattractive for the Federal Reserve to restart QE, the current economic weakness means this cannot be ruled out. 4 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **24 October 2011** The fact that inflation seems to be under more control than was the case earlier this year may also make QE more likely. One of the arguments against QE is that it may generate significant levels of inflation. With recession looming in North America and throughout Europe, the spectre of deflation may be more worrying and QE might yet be adopted at least in part due to this inflationary drive. The current focus is slowly shifting towards fear of deflation._ Although the stress in the world’s financial system is very clear to see, we remain _relatively_ relaxed about the likely outcome for the European debt crisis and its effect on the world economy. A Greek default seems extremely likely or almost certain but, if this is (eventually) carried out in an orderly fashion, this could reduce the risk of contagion of other more solvent economies. Although a number of banks seem likely to be recapitalised (following the rescue of Dexia which was the sixteenth largest European bank), we feel that the Lehman/Bear Sterns experience makes it likely that most (or all) banks would be rescued by national governments if the only other choice were a disorderly insolvency. Recession seems almost certain in some d

eveloped economies but, unless this is accompanied by a banking crisis or the break-up of the Euro, this could be a relatively shallow recession in most countries. In this base case scenario, the global economy should continue to grow and outright risk aversion should gradually be replaced by more reasoned valuation of assets. While we accept that there are significant potential downsides to this scenario, this should be bullish for the more industrial of the precious metals. We remain bullish of gold from a risk aversion perspective and for the same reasons we have been positive so far this year: Central Bank buying, cheap money, inflation fears and asset diversification. 5 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **24 October 2011** ## **Gold** September was a challenging month in the gold market for traders and analysts alike. Gold climbed from just over $1,600 an ounce at the end of July to new all-time highs above $1,900 in late August before crashing back to $1,710 only a few days later. Enough bulls remained active to drive gold to another new peak of $1,920 on the 6th of September. In this hugely volatile market, $2,000 came into view but, equally, $1,700 did not seem too far away. The bulls blinked first and, as the Dollar strengthened on an understandable wariness over holding too many Euros, gold slipped back to settle around $1,800 from the 15th of September to the 22nd. The US Federal Reserve then launched “Operation Twist”. This aims to twist the yield curve, lowering longer term interest rates by selling short term bonds and buying longer term bonds. However, the relatively unambitious scale of the programme underwhelmed investors. The Federal Reserve’s apparent realisation of the highly fragile state of the US economy (and indeed of the global economy) also unnerved the market, driving selling of all kinds of assets including gold which tumbled to $1,550 on the 26th. As so often, the price movements seemed somewhat overextended and gold rallied to end the month above $1,600 again on its way to a mid-October $1,670. Gold Price(USD/oz)

**_Figure 4_** _: The gold price hit new record highs and threatened $2,000 at the start of September before crashing lower._ After trading in this huge monthly range, it seems entirely reasonable to question whether anything has changed in the gold market. Our feeling is that the move upwards was overextended and that the move downwards in reply went too far. It does not seem that many of the drivers of a higher gold price have weakened in recent weeks. Indeed, the Swiss Government’s decision to attempt to tie the Swiss Franc to the Euro removed one possible safe haven and should have increased gold’s attractiveness to investors. The fall back in the gol

d price has – temporarily at least – reinvigorated jewellery buying in India and slowed scrap flows. ETF holdings were remarkably stable considering the scale of the price movements. Although QE3 seems further away than before, interest rates seem set to remain at low levels for an extended period of time and a Greek default seems ever more likely. Overall, therefore, the reasons to hold gold seem every bit as convincing as they were a month ago, although investor confidence may have been dented and the speed of any future price rise might be a little more leisurely than was the case last time. Even though inflation figures seem to be trending downwards in many markets, inflation remains uncomfortably high, macroeconomic risk is widespread throughout the global financial system and money is set to remain cheap for some time to come. We thus continue to be bullish for the gold price over the next twelve months. 6 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **24 October 2011** ### **Investor and jewellery demand for gold** Physical demand for gold remains strong. The Indian gold market is highly seasonal and very price sensitive. With the festival season, a period of strong consumer buying, approaching, the fall in the gold price in late September was welcome in terms of driving additional demand despite a weaker Rupee. The Bombay Bullion Association estimated that imports of gold during that period might be 100-150 tonnes compared to 90 tonnes one year earlier. Annual imports could climb over 1,000 tonnes, an increase on the 958 tonnes reported in 2010. Additionally, new has emerged that the Bombay Bullion Association is planning to launch an exchange traded fund (ETF) in gold within the next six months. This will generate some extra demand for gold although, since ETFs or ETF-like products are already available within India, the additional buying will be relatively limited in scale. Within China, gold sales were also strong in September, partly aided by buying ahead of the October Golden Week holidays. Margin increases have dampened down some of the enthusiasm in the futures markets on both Shanghai exchanges but physical trading on the Shanghai Gold Exchange is running at record volumes for the year-to-date. Metal premiums have also been maintained at a relatively high level, in accordance with indications of strong jewellery demand as well. Cumulative SGE sales of Au YTD

**_Figure 7_** _: ...but futures investors were driven out of the market in much greater numbers._ On COMEX, net long speculative interest had been decreasing even before the gold price started its move to further record highs. It fell from 33 million ounces at the start of August to a low of 19.6 million ounces at the start of October. Short interest peaked around the middle of the month as gold started to come down from the earlier highs but actually diminished through September. A decrease in long interest was the more important factor with many positions closed in the week to the 27th of September when interest fell by 5.2 million ounces. This was the largest fall since August 2008 when the price stood closer to $800. Given the level of bullishness still present in the market, speculative positioning does not seem overextended and further upwards moves in the price could well follow. **_Figure 8_** _: Gold can even be purchased at currency exchanges at Munich airport, demonstrating its new-found mainstream appeal…._ Finally, we note that coin and bar demand remains strong in Europe and, more generally, worldwide as investors look to diversify their assets to address

perceived economic risk and continue to buy into the long term rising price.

### **LBMA Conference** 

The annual LBMA conference was held (jointly with the LPPM) in Montreal from the 18th to the 20th of September. Few new opinions or facts were revealed relating to the gold market which was held with gold trading close to $1,800 per ounce. At the start of the conference, attendees forecast a gold price of $2,075 at the time of the next conference (November 2012). By the end of the conference, this forecast had fallen to a still bullish $2,019. However, although the mood was positive, when compared to a year earlier, the conference attendees were rather less universally bullish on this occasion. 



**_Figure 9_** _: ….although larger coins like this one seen at the LBMA conference in Montreal attract a more select clientele._ 

### **The gold-platinum price premium** 

We discuss the existence and the impact of gold’s current price premium over platinum from the point of view of platinum later in this report. However, there is also the possibility that this premium will impact upon the gold market too. 

From an investment point of view, platinum is widely considered to be a more valuable metal than gold and the move towards parity in price terms drove some trading on the platinum:gold ratio with buying of platinum and selling of gold. With the ratio having continued to move in the same direction, the simple 1:1 trade may be less important but buying platinum and selling gold continues to be a popular trade. However, we note that given the comparative size of the two markets, this is more likely to be a positive for platinum prices than a drag on gold prices. The platinum market is simply not large enough to have a major impact on the gold price through this linkage mechanism. 

From a jewellery point of view, the same comparison of market size indicates that, while platinum may gain some market share due to trading at a lower price than gold, the impact on the gold market is likely to be much smaller. We do believe that a lower platinum metal price (in comparison with the gold price) is positive for platinum demand and will be very slightly negative for gold demand. However, this will apply only in countries where there is a platinum jewellery market of sufficient size to compete (China, Europe, Japan and North America). 

In India, platinum jewellery is a small but growing market and the price differential between the two metals will be unimportant. In China, the gold market is much larger than the platinum market so the impact on gold demand will be limited. The European, Japanese and North American markets are much less clear cut. Here, gold represents the majority of the (non-silver) jewellery market but is seldom sold as 24 carat metal. Instead, it is

often seen at 14-22 carats (and sometimes lower) or 58 per cent to 92 per cent purity. Platinum alloys are typically at the higher end of the purity scale. So, at current prices the precious metal costs associated with either metal may in fact be close to equal. With platinum pieces often attracting a greater mark-up, manufacturers and retailers may be driven to use more of this metal, denting gold jewellery demand in these markets but, overall, having limited impact on the gold market. 

### **Official sector activity** 

Excluding the IMF sales which took place last year, signatories to the third Central Bank Gold Agreement (CBGA3) have sold only a little over a tonne of metal in the past year. Total sales in the second year of the agreement were 53.3 tonnes, well short of the 400 tonnes which was permitted. Most of these sales were part of the IMF’s well-publicised disposal of 403 tonnes. Although the ECB, Greece, Portugal and Spain are signatories to this agreement we do not expect to see significant levels of gold sales from CBGA3 banks in the next year, despite the obvious debt and budgetary issues. 

Elsewhere, Central Banks were buyers. In August (the most recent data available in most cases), Thailand added 10 tonnes to its reserves, Bolivia bought roughly 7 tonnes of gold and Russia purchased another 4 tonnes of gold from its domestic market. 

Additionally, we saw two stories pointing out the perceived importance of gold in national economic security terms. A direct democracy initiative in Switzerland seeks to make the Swiss National Bank repatriate any gold it owns overseas to Swiss vaults and to maintain a minimum level of gold as a percentage of its national reserves. The Venezuelan Government also intervened in its national market by banning gold exports, attempting to partnationalise the industry and repatriate its reserves where these are held abroad. While these may not be typical viewpoints on gold as a reserve asset, when added to concerns over the health of the Dollar and the Euro, we see Central Bank buying as likely to persist for some time. 

### **Production news** 

Given the high level of the gold price compared to most mine costs, it is not surprising to see plans for expansion of mine output from many companies. AngloGold Ashanti recently confirmed its plans to increase its output from just under 4.5 million ounces of gold this year to an annual 5.5 million ounces by 2014 with all of this expansion outside South Africa. 

At the start of October, Banro poured the first gold from its new Twangiza mine in South Kivu province in the Democratic Republic of Congo. 

In Mongolia, Ivanhoe’s huge copper/gold mine at Oyu Tolgoi (scheduled to produce 650,000 ounces of gold per year with first production starting in 2013) reached the midpoint of the first phase of its construction in September. However, as we noted in a recent report, high metal prices have encouraged many governments to attempt to renegotiate the financial

terms of mining investment in their territory (as with Venezuela above). The Mongolian Government has made some initial comments on its wish to renegotiate commercial terms in its favour. While we do not expect this to prevent the development of the mine, we do see this as part of the trend towards asymmetrical risk for investors in mining operations in many jurisdictions, something that will constrain supply side response to high prices and is, in principle, bullish for the prices of most metals. 10 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **24 October 2011** ## **Silver** The silver price was affected by the same factors as the other precious metal prices during September. As with gold, it slowly softened throughout much of the month before plunging lower from the 22nd to the 26th. Only a year ago it would have seemed almost unimaginable for silver to trade in a $10 range during a single month. In September, it peaked at roughly $43.30 on the 2nd of September and fell to a low of $26.10 on the 26th, a range of more than $17. Needless to say, this move was not driven by fundamentals but rather by risk aversion and a strengthening US Dollar. Silver Price (USD/oz)

**_Figure 10_** _: The silver price fell as low as $26.10 on the 26th of September to test investors’ resolve._ The gold:silver ratio moved strongly against silver during the month, particularly following the Operation Twist announcement. Essentially, this is a continuation of the trend that has been in place since late April. As the stress in the global banking system has increased and concerns over the Euro have intensified, gold has performed its traditional safe haven role rather better than silver. Examination of movements in the silver price last year suggests that part of the strength of silver was driven by physical demand for four nines metal whether from ETF investors, the photovoltaic market or from coin demand. Photovoltaic demand is a little softer than in late 2010 and, although coin demand is strong (see below), ETF buying is much less of a driving force. As a result, pure speculative interest is of greater importance in driving the price. The reduction of investor involvement can be seen in the narrowing of the differential between indium and silver. We expect to see stronger physical demand as we move into next year and for silver to narrow the gold:silver ratio. However, before that point, continued economic and financial woes should see gold outperforming silver. Figure 11 : Market stress

**_Figure 13_** _: Silver coin sales are at a record level this year._ The behaviour of ETF investors is a little different, however. Total exchange traded fund holdings of silver changed little throughout August and September, fluctuating only between 450 and 460 million ounces of metal. This is in sharp contrast to the situation in 2010 when heavy buying of silver through ETFs started in September, helping the price in its meteoric rise. However, little selling was seen from the ETFs despite the plunge in the price. Some 2.5 million ounces of metal was redeemed in the week leading up to the 23rd of September as the price started to fall but investors mostly hung on, unlike in early May when they sold almost 40 million ounces of silver after the price failed to breach the $50 level. Total holdings stood at 459.3 million ounces at the end of September and, for the year as a whole, ETFs have acted as a source of supply of roughly 28 million ounces. This illustrates that ETF investment is not always a source of fresh demand in the precious metal markets. Although the silver price may currently look disappointing compared to its late 12 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **24 October 2011** April peaks, it should be noted that silver is trading a little above where it started the year. **_Figure 15_** _: ….but selling of futures positions was constant and heavy._ ### **Photovoltaic demand** Following last year’s bonanza for photovoltaic (PV) system and component manufacturers, many companies moved to add manufacturing capacity in anticipation of another grandstand year in 2011. Unfortunately, the global economic recovery has faltered and slowed considerably. Most of the new installations of PV systems in 2010 were in Europe with German and Spanish consumers responsible for a majority of European demand. Unsurprisingly, this source of demand has slowed this year as subsidies have been cut and construction of new buildings remains at depressed levels. In the UK too, a reduction 13 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **24 October 2011** in solar panel prices and high subsidies made PV a very attractive financial investment. Unfortunately, the Government looks set to reduce subsidies here too. As a result, the PV industry has been faced with overcapacity this year and the prices of photovoltaic systems have fallen sharply. While this has hurt the industry’s profitability and driven some consolidation, it has also triggered renewed interest in installing PV technology in North America. Government subsidies are important here too with California responsi

ble for more than half of US development activity in this sector due to its subsidy programme. Other markets look set to absorb some of the slack left by weak European demand and the number of units shipped is expected to climb but, depending on the state of the world economy, the annual growth rate could range between 15 and 50 per cent. The likely result is that silver demand should increase more quickly in 2011 than in 2010, providing more support to the silver price than was the case this year when PV demand growth rates slipped dramatically. 14 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **24 October 2011** ## **Platinum** The fall in the platinum price in September was sudden and disorientating for the market in general. Platinum started the month firmly at $1,850 and inched higher to $1,895 on the 6th before starting to slide as the Dollar strengthened and fear once again set in across the market. $1,800 provided some support towards the middle of the month but platinum slipped through and the selling that followed the announcement of Operation Twist hit platinum very hard indeed, with the price lurching below $1,500 on the 26th of the month. Since that point, the platinum price has recovered over the $1,500 mark but only by a small amount, partly due to the week-long closure of the Shanghai Gold Exchange for the October National Day holidays, which removed a source of physical demand. low levels of profit available from mining for platinum in South Africa.

A comparison of rates of return of project finance for mining based on current mineral prices show platinum mining, in general, to be a less attractive investment opportunity than many other metals at today’s prices. When country risk - whether from South Africa or Zimbabwe - is added into the mix and further uncertainty is included simply due to the up to one decade long timespan of getting a deep level mine into full production, it is not clear how many new platinum mines will be commissioned in the next few years (although there are currently numerous new projects in the pipeline). Indeed, with platinum close to $1,500 and rhodium and palladium prices having weakened too, the South African mining industry is operating at close to breakeven on average when replacement capital expenditure is included. 

In this situation, should prices remain depressed for an extended period, there are a limited number of scenarios: platinum output could be maintained if the Rand weakened, or if by-product prices climbed significantly; demand destruction could be seen (although this could require higher metal prices); or platinum production could start to wither. 

Although there is continual pressure from consumers to reduce their precious metal usage, we feel that current prices are not especially problematic for the majority of platinum users. The metal price is some way below its historical highs and gold and rhodium prices are at comparable levels, reducing the incentive to switch to the use of these other metals in applications where this is possible. There is of course, ongoing substitution of platinum by palladium in the autocatalyst sector: this will continue at current price levels but will not result in significant further demand destruction. The most likely drive for lower metal demand would be an economic crisis or global recession, something which we do not currently expect to occur. 

By-product prices (mainly palladium and rhodium but also other metals including gold, ruthenium and iridium) seem to be in the same situation as platinum with current prices performing weakly partly due to fragile investor interest and uncertainty over industrial demand. We believe that the palladium price will eventually rebound from current levels and provide some respite for the South African platinum producers but that this process may be slow. 

In more normal economic times, the persistently high level of inflation in South Africa and its export-centred economy should eventually lead to a weaker currency. However, a general lack of desire to own Dollars and the other major reserve currencies may yet support the Rand in the shorter, two year timeframe. Additionally, any recovery in the global economy could support commodity prices, attracting further capital inflows and firming the Rand. Alth

ough we do expect the Rand to weaken over the medium term, there is therefore no certainty that a weak Rand will come to the rescue of the mining sector. The behaviour of the supply side is therefore of importance in determining the metal price. While there may be warnings over the profitability of the industry, few producers will be keen to make the first move in trimming output. Nonetheless, as in 2008-2009, low prices would eventually result in the closure of a normal of open pits, half levels and individual shafts although few whole mines could be expected to be closed. It is therefore possible for the platinum price to remain below the cost of production for some period of time and we do not see the cost of production as a short term source of support for the price. Nonetheless, were prices to stay at close to their current levels, a supply side response could eventually be expected. This should support platinum above the cost of production in the longer term. Given the above-inflation cost increases in salaries, electricity, safety costs and mining equipment prices, this means that we can only be bullish for platinum prices in Dollar terms over the next three years. 16 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **24 October 2011** ### **Fear gauge #1** The platinum:gold price ratio has come into regular discussion in recent weeks since it slipped below 1:1 during September. We do not believe there is any fundamental significance to this ratio, given the wide differences in the market dynamics of each metal. However, we do accept that there are psychological and branding issues that might be expected to support the platinum price at or above the level of the gold price. Specifically, in many consumers’ minds, platinum is perceived as the superior metal in terms of brand attributes. This can be seen in various forms, from the greater music sales required for a platinum disc compared to a gold disc in the recording industry to the selling price of a platinum watch compared to an analogous gold model. Some other sectors, however, have seen slowing growth, contributing to the recent price weakness. 21 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **24 October 2011** ### **Automotive demand** In mid-September, the Chinese Government announced changes to its environmental subsidy programme for smaller vehicles. These amendments were planned to take effect at the start of October. Previously, these subsidies could reduce the purchase price of a new car by roughly RMB 3,000 (or roughly US$500). However, a tightening of the eligibility rules means that only the vehicles with the very best fuel economy will now qualify. Previously over 400 different models were included in this programme but this figure will now fall to below 40. Many consumers responded logically and brought forward purchases which might otherwise have occurred in early October into September. As a result, we expect relatively healthy sales figures for Q3 in China but to see a slowdown in growth in Q4. For the year as a whole, the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers is now expecting growth of below 5

per cent in vehicle sales. In Brazil, the Government moved to increase the IPI tax (essentially a value-added tax) on imported passenger vehicles by 30 per cent from September until the end of 2012. This move, which looks suspiciously like an import tariff will not be applied to vehicles manufactured either in Mexico or in the Mercosur/Mercosul region. Imports have risen 16 per cent of the car market in 2009 to 23 per cent this year as the Brazilian Real has strengthened and the impositions of such a tax is a strong negative for the car market, which might well contract in the final quarter of the year instead of continuing to grow. In Japan, there were some positive signs in the automotive sector as car production rose above August 2010 levels during August 2011. This was the first year-on-year growth in output since September 2010 and marks a return to normal levels of production following March’s triple disaster. It would, however, be wrong to assume that output has fully normalised. Component shortages still persist in some subsectors and output of some specific models remains impaired. Until all vehicle models become widely available once again, sales of Japanese cars are set to underperform compared to their full potential. Monthly Japanese light duty vehicle

Additionally, September marked the third anniversary of the collapse of Lehman Brothers, marking the worst phase of the global economic crisis. Since that point, new car sales and leasing have been depressed. All positivity was extracted from investors by the decline in the price to below $600 an ounce. At the start of the year, sentiment for palladium was almost universally bullish with expectations of further significant price rises. However, the failure to meet these had eroded investor confidence. Whilst we feel that a further push towards $1,000 per ounce will happen in the next few years, investor buying is unlikely to emerge again in significant volumes this year. However, once prices and expectations have been reset at the start of 2012, the scene could be set for a renewed assault on these higher price levels. As the price fell, September therefore progressively provided more of a selling opportunity for investors who were already long, whether in ETFs or on the futures exchanges. On NYMEX, net long speculative interest fell from 1.41 million ounces in early September to only 580,000 ounces at the start of October.
